scope_note: A sourced comparison of speaker-verification metrics, embedding models, and packaged verification APIs -- "does this cloned/synthesized voice actually sound like the target speaker, and can I trust an automated same-speaker check." Covers the metric itself (SECS and its canonical encoder), raw embedding models you run yourself, and hosted verification APIs. This project runs no speaker-verification benchmarks of its own; EER/accuracy figures are attributed and marked accordingly.
method_note: Every claim is checked against the vendor's own documentation or source repository before publication, then adversarially audited in a second pass that actively tries to refute each field rather than confirm it, followed by a dedicated facet-recheck pass verifying every facet against the row's own (possibly-corrected) text. EER/accuracy figures are mostly vendor-reported and marked verification: vendor-claim or mixed unless independently confirmed.

systems.name: SECS (Speaker Encoder Cosine Similarity)
systems.licence: N/A — a scoring formula, not licensed software
systems.price_note: Free — it's arithmetic; cost is whichever speaker encoder you compute it with
systems.method: Cosine similarity between two speaker-embedding vectors (reference audio vs. synthesized audio), where the embeddings come from a separately-trained speaker encoder — most commonly Resemblyzer's d-vector model, though newer papers substitute a WavLM-TDNN or ECAPA-TDNN encoder and still call the resulting number SECS or SIM
systems.availability: An open, widely-reimplemented definition rather than a distributed package; the canonical implementation (via Resemblyzer) is open source
systems.best_for: A cheap, reproducible objective proxy for 'does this cloned voice sound like the target speaker' in TTS/voice-cloning papers and eval pipelines, reported alongside MOS/SMOS listening tests
systems.watch: SECS is only as trustworthy as the encoder computing it. Most papers still use the small, unmaintained Resemblyzer d-vector model (256-dim, trained years ago), so a high SECS number does not guarantee agreement with a modern speaker-verification system or a human listener — and it is not directly comparable to SIM-o/SIM-r scores computed with a WavLM-TDNN or ECAPA-TDNN encoder, even though papers sometimes report both under similar-sounding names.
systems.standout: The most widely reported objective speaker-similarity number in the TTS/voice-cloning literature, precisely because it is cheap, encoder-agnostic in principle, and requires no human raters
systems.adoption: Reported as a standard objective speaker-similarity metric across dozens of zero-shot TTS papers since 2021, when YourTTS formally named and popularized SECS (via Resemblyzer); the same cosine-similarity-of-speaker-embeddings technique appears earlier under other names (e.g., Attentron, 2020, calls it 'speaker similarity,' not SECS), and SECS is now the common label used by it and many follow-ups.
systems.verification_note: The name and formula are consistent across multiple published TTS papers (e.g. YourTTS, which formally defines and uses SECS via Resemblyzer), but no single primary source 'owns' the metric — it is a community convention, not a spec.

systems.name: Resemblyzer
systems.method: 256-dim speaker-embedding encoder (GE2E-style LSTM d-vector model, spun out of the Real-Time-Voice-Cloning project); cosine/L2 distance between embeddings scores voice similarity, and the same embeddings support speaker diarization and basic fake-speech screening.
systems.availability: Open source Python package (PyPI: resemblyzer; GitHub: resemble-ai/Resemblyzer); runs on CPU or GPU
systems.best_for: Fast, install-and-go voice-similarity checks in a Python script or a TTS eval pipeline — VoiceEncoder().embed_utterance(wav) is the entire API — especially retrofitting into SV2TTS / Real-Time-Voice-Cloning-style pipelines.
systems.watch: No commits or PyPI releases since v0.1.4 in October 2023 (about three years stale as of this writing), and no EER or accuracy figure on a named benchmark is published anywhere in the repo — its only quality evidence is a small qualitative demo. Treat any SECS number from it as a legacy, low-resolution baseline rather than a state-of-the-art speaker check.
systems.standout: The de facto reference implementation behind the 'SECS' number reported across the TTS literature — ubiquity, not accuracy, is what keeps it relevant — via the simplest possible API for voice-similarity scripting.
systems.adoption: 3.3k GitHub stars / 483 forks (resemble-ai/Resemblyzer); cited as the canonical SECS encoder across dozens of zero-shot TTS papers (confirmed for YourTTS and Attentron specifically)
systems.verification_note: No EER or accuracy number on a named benchmark is published by the project — its only quality evidence is a single qualitative demo notebook, not a named-benchmark result.

systems.name: ECAPA-TDNN (SpeechBrain)
systems.method: TDNN with SE-Res2Blocks, channel- and context-dependent attention, and attentive statistics pooling, trained on VoxCeleb1+VoxCeleb2 with AAM-softmax, 192-dim embeddings; same/different-speaker decisions made via cosine similarity between embeddings.
systems.availability: Self-hosted — pip install speechbrain, or load the speechbrain/spkrec-ecapa-voxceleb checkpoint directly from Hugging Face; requires the SpeechBrain Python toolkit to run.
systems.best_for: The default off-the-shelf same/different-speaker cosine-similarity check for open-source voice-cloning eval and diarization pipelines — a stronger, actively-maintained encoder than legacy Resemblyzer, backed by a published, named-benchmark EER.
systems.watch: The published 0.80% EER is a single number tied to one May 2021 release tag, with no confidence interval or trial-list version noted — treat it as a reference point, not a guarantee on your own data. It is also only one of two SpeechBrain-reported figures on the same VoxCeleb1-O test list: 0.80% WITH score normalization (on the model card itself), vs. 0.90% WITHOUT score normalization (from a separate SpeechBrain GitHub recipe results table, not the model card) — two scoring variants of one test set, not two different benchmarks.
systems.standout: The most widely reused open speaker-embedding checkpoint in the ecosystem (~1.7M Hugging Face downloads/month — more than double the next comparable open checkpoint, pyannote/embedding) — it functions as the de facto baseline that other tools and papers in this category benchmark against.
systems.benchmark_note: 0.80% EER on VoxCeleb1-O (the same list the SpeechBrain HF model card calls 'VoxCeleb1-test (Cleaned)') WITH score normalization — the figure published on the model card itself. Without score normalization, SpeechBrain's own separate GitHub VoxCeleb/SpeakerRec recipe results table reports 0.90% EER on the same list; both are trained on VoxCeleb1+2. These are two scoring variants of one test set, not two different benchmarks, and only the 0.80% figure is on the model card this row cites as source_url.
systems.adoption: ~1.7M downloads/month on Hugging Face (speechbrain/spkrec-ecapa-voxceleb), per the model page's live download counter as of this audit; the SpeechBrain toolkit itself has active commits through mid-2026.
systems.verification_note: Licence (Apache-2.0) and embedding dimension (192, lin_neurons in hyperparams.yaml) are confirmed directly on the Hugging Face model card. The 0.80% EER figure is the one published on that model card; the 0.90% figure comes from SpeechBrain's separate GitHub VoxCeleb/SpeakerRec recipe results table (without score normalization), not the model card itself. Both are SpeechBrain self-reports, not independently reproduced here.

systems.name: WavLM-TDNN speaker verification (Microsoft UniSpeech)
systems.licence: CC BY-SA 3.0 (Attribution-ShareAlike, via the microsoft/UniSpeech repo)
systems.price_note: Free, open source (weights + inference code in the UniSpeech GitHub repo)
systems.method: WavLM-large self-supervised speech representation, fine-tuned with an x-vector head and Additive Margin Softmax for speaker verification; cosine similarity between embeddings gives the SIM-o/SIM-r speaker-similarity score reported by VALL-E, VALL-E 2, NaturalSpeech 3, and ByteDance's Seed-TTS Eval
systems.availability: Open source checkpoint + code at github.com/microsoft/UniSpeech (downstreams/speaker_verification); a smaller variant — WavLM Base+, a separately pretrained model rather than a distillation of WavLM-large — is also on Hugging Face as microsoft/wavlm-base-plus-sv
systems.best_for: The current de facto standard speaker-similarity encoder for zero-shot TTS papers reporting SIM-o/SIM-r, when you want a stronger and more independently-benchmarked check than SECS/Resemblyzer
systems.watch: Distributed under Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 3.0 — an unusual, copyleft-flavored term for a model checkpoint, worth reading before folding it into a commercial eval pipeline. Also, many zero-shot TTS papers describe using 'a WavLM-TDNN checkpoint fine-tuned for speaker verification' without publishing the exact weights, so SIM-o/SIM-r numbers quoted across different papers are not always produced by literally the same model.
systems.standout: The underlying WavLM-large model topped the VoxSRC 2021 and 2022 speaker-verification challenge leaderboards, giving SIM-o/SIM-r more independent pedigree than SECS's aging Resemblyzer baseline
systems.benchmark_note: EER 0.431% (Vox1-O), 0.538% (Vox1-E), 1.154% (Vox1-H) for WavLM-large, per the microsoft/UniSpeech speaker-verification README
systems.adoption: The speaker-similarity encoder behind the SIM-o/SIM-r metric reported in VALL-E, VALL-E 2, NaturalSpeech 3, and ByteDance's Seed-TTS Eval benchmark suite
systems.verification_note: Licence terms and VoxCeleb EER figures were read directly from the microsoft/UniSpeech repo; the EER numbers are Microsoft's own reported results, not independently reproduced.

systems.name: WeSpeaker
systems.licence: Apache-2.0 (toolkit code); CC-BY-4.0 on VoxCeleb-trained checkpoints
systems.price_note: Free, open source (pip install or GitHub)
systems.method: Research-and-production speaker-embedding toolkit covering multiple architectures (ResNet up to 293 layers, ECAPA-TDNN, CAM++, ERes2Net, ReDimNet, SSL-frontend variants), with training recipes plus an ONNX/C++ runtime and a Triton inference-server demo for production deployment (TensorRT export included).
systems.availability: Self-hosted — clone wenet-e2e/wespeaker; pretrained checkpoints published on Hugging Face under the Wespeaker org; ONNX/TensorRT export and a Triton inference-server demo included
systems.best_for: Teams that want a maintained, production-grade toolkit — real serving/export support and diarization built in — to train, fine-tune, or deploy their own speaker-verification embedding model, covering everything from a lightweight ResNet34 to a 293-layer deep R-vector.
systems.watch: It's a toolkit with many recipes and checkpoints of varying vintage rather than one model — the headline EER numbers are its best-tuned VoxCeleb1-O recipes (AS-Norm + large-margin fine-tuning), not what a default training run produces.
systems.standout: The broadest open architecture zoo in this category, plus an explicit production runtime (ONNX/C++/TensorRT/Triton) — WeSpeaker's own ResNet34 checkpoint is also what pyannote.audio wraps for its diarization pipeline, and it has been used as a VoxSRC-challenge baseline system.
systems.benchmark_note: VoxCeleb1-O (cleaned), with AS-Norm + large-margin fine-tuning: ResNet34 0.72% EER, ECAPA-TDNN (c1024) 0.73% EER, 293-layer Deep R-vector 0.45% EER (minDCF 0.069 for the ResNet34 recipe), per the project's own recipe results.
systems.adoption: 1.4k GitHub stars (wenet-e2e/wespeaker); maintained by the WeNet community with a real industrial co-affiliation (Tencent's Ethereal Audio Lab, per the project's own ICASSP paper). Wrapped into pyannote.audio as pyannote/wespeaker-voxceleb-resnet34-LM, and used as a baseline system in VoxSRC2023 challenge submissions (arXiv:2306.15161).
systems.verification_note: Licence, feature list (ONNX/TensorRT/Triton runtime, architecture zoo), and active-development status are confirmed directly on the repo; the VoxCeleb EER/minDCF figures are the project's own self-reported recipe results, not independently reproduced for this survey.

systems.name: TitaNet-Large (NVIDIA NeMo)
systems.method: 1D depth-wise separable convolutions with Squeeze-and-Excitation global-context blocks and channel-attention statistics pooling ("t-vector"); trained on a broad English mix — VoxCeleb1/2, Fisher, Switchboard, LibriSpeech, and NIST SRE (2004–2010)
systems.availability: Self-hosted via the NVIDIA NeMo toolkit (nemo_asr.models.EncDecSpeakerLabelModel.from_pretrained), checkpoint on NGC and Hugging Face
systems.best_for: Verification and diarization inside an NVIDIA/NeMo-based pipeline, where its 192-d embeddings feed straight into NeMo's own diarization stack
systems.watch: No adoption/usage figures are published for this specific checkpoint, and its EER numbers are NVIDIA's own reported figures only, never independently reproduced. Using it means pulling in the full NeMo toolkit as a dependency rather than a lightweight standalone package -- there is no NVIDIA-published CPU-only or reduced-footprint inference guidance for this specific (Large) checkpoint.
systems.standout: One of the few embedding models trained on a genuinely broad mix of corpora (VoxCeleb, Fisher, Switchboard, LibriSpeech, NIST SRE) rather than VoxCeleb alone, and it ships pre-integrated with NeMo's diarization pipeline.
systems.benchmark_note: 0.66% EER on the VoxCeleb1 cleaned trial list (veri_test2.txt) per the model card; the original TitaNet paper (Koluguri et al., ICASSP 2022) reports 0.68% EER on VoxCeleb1
systems.verification_note: EER figures are NVIDIA's own reported numbers (model card and original paper); not independently reproduced for this survey.

systems.name: pyannote speaker embedding (WeSpeaker ResNet34)
systems.method: ResNet34 with statistics pooling (WeSpeaker architecture), wrapped for pyannote.audio's Model/Inference API; same/different-speaker decisions via cosine distance between 256-d embeddings
systems.availability: Self-hosted — pip install pyannote.audio (>=3.1); checkpoint pyannote/wespeaker-voxceleb-resnet34-LM on Hugging Face
systems.best_for: Speaker verification/embedding extraction inside a pyannote.audio pipeline — it's the actual embedding model behind pyannote's widely-used speaker-diarization-3.1 pipeline
systems.watch: This is a thin wrapper around WeSpeaker's own ResNet34-LM checkpoint, not an independent architecture, and its card publishes no EER/accuracy figure of its own. A 2.8% EER is sometimes quoted for "pyannote speaker embedding" and misattributed to this model — that number actually belongs to the separate, architecturally unrelated pyannote/embedding model (SincNet/x-vector, not ResNet34). For reference, WeSpeaker's own published results for this architecture family (ResNet34-TSTP-emb256 on VoxCeleb1-O) are far lower than 2.8%: ~0.87% untuned, ~0.72% with large-margin fine-tuning plus AS-Norm — though that exact figure is not confirmed to be for this specific pretrained checkpoint.
systems.standout: It's the default embedding model inside pyannote.audio's speaker-diarization-3.1 pipeline, one of the most widely deployed open-source diarization stacks, so it gets exercised at large scale beyond standalone verification use.
systems.benchmark_note: Not stated on this model's own card (verified: the README contains no EER/accuracy figures). The 2.8% EER sometimes quoted for "pyannote speaker embedding" belongs to a different, older pyannote model (pyannote/embedding, a SincNet/x-vector architecture) and does not apply to this WeSpeaker ResNet34 wrapper.
systems.adoption: Default embedding model in pyannote/speaker-diarization-3.1, one of the most-used open-source diarization pipelines on Hugging Face
systems.verification_note: License (CC-BY-4.0), architecture/method, and its role as the default embedding in pyannote/speaker-diarization-3.1 were independently confirmed against this model's own README and the diarization pipeline's config.yaml (embedding: pyannote/wespeaker-voxceleb-resnet34-LM). No EER/accuracy figure is published on this model's card; a 2.8% EER previously listed here belongs to a different pyannote model and was removed.

systems.name: WavLM-Base-Plus-SV (Microsoft)
systems.method: Self-supervised WavLM Transformer encoder (pretrained on 94k hours of speech: Libri-Light, GigaSpeech, VoxPopuli) fine-tuned on VoxCeleb1 with an X-Vector head and Additive Margin Softmax loss; verified via cosine similarity between 512-d embeddings
systems.best_for: Teams already using WavLM/SSL representations elsewhere in a pipeline (e.g. ASR) who want a speaker embedding from the same encoder family, rather than a dedicated speaker-embedding-first model
systems.watch: The weights are CC-BY-SA-3.0, a share-alike license — unlike the Apache-2.0/CC-BY-4.0 checkpoints elsewhere in this category, derivatives may need to be released under the same terms, which is worth a legal read before shipping it in a closed product. Its own model card also publishes no EER for this specific checkpoint; the WavLM paper's headline VoxCeleb1 EER figures (down to 0.33% Vox1-O) are for the much larger WavLM-Large checkpoint, not this Base+ one.
systems.standout: The only entry in this category built on a general-purpose self-supervised speech encoder rather than a supervised speaker-embedding-first architecture, so the same backbone can in principle be reused for other speech tasks.
systems.released: 2021 (WavLM paper); SV checkpoint fine-tuned and published separately by Microsoft on Hugging Face
systems.verification_note: No EER is published for this specific checkpoint; only a similarity-threshold recommendation (0.86, described as dataset-dependent) appears on the model card.

systems.name: Azure AI Speaker Recognition (Microsoft)
systems.price_note: Retired — was consumption-billed under Azure AI Speech before shutdown; no current pricing exists
systems.method: Text-dependent verification (passphrase + voice signature match), text-independent verification, and text-independent identification via the Azure Cognitive Services Speech SDK
systems.availability: Discontinued. The underlying service was retired 2025-09-30 and speaker-recognition support was removed from the Speech SDK in release 1.47 (Nov 2025)
systems.best_for: Historical reference only — do not build new integrations on this; included because it was one of the only hyperscaler-native speaker-verification APIs
systems.watch: Fully retired: Microsoft's own Speech SDK 1.47 release notes state 'Removed speaker recognition support due to the service retirement.' Microsoft points migrating users toward real-time diarization, which separates speakers in a recording but does not verify identity against an enrolled voiceprint. A hyperscaler-native alternative does still exist, though: Google Cloud's Speaker ID (GA since October 2021, integrated with Contact Center AI / Dialogflow CX) performs text-independent verification against enrolled voiceprints, so Azure's gap is not industry-wide.
systems.standout: Was a hyperscaler-native (not third-party) speaker verification API. Its retirement — alongside AWS's Connect Voice ID, which ends support for existing customers in 2026 — leaves Google Cloud's Speaker ID as the only major hyperscaler-native speaker-verification offering still active; this is a partial, not industry-wide, pull-back.
systems.released: GA in Speech SDK 1.19.0 (Nov 2021); service retired 2025-09-30; SDK support removed in Speech SDK 1.47 (Nov 2025)
systems.verification_note: Retirement and SDK-removal dates confirmed directly on Microsoft's own Speech service release notes.

systems.name: Amazon Connect Voice ID (AWS)
systems.price_note: Discontinued — was billed per Voice ID enrollment/verification transaction inside Amazon Connect; no current pricing exists
systems.method: Real-time, passive text-independent voiceprint verification embedded in Amazon Connect call flows: ~30s of net speech to enroll, ~10s to verify against the claimed identity or a fraudster watchlist
systems.availability: Discontinued. New customer access was blocked from 2025-05-20 and AWS ended all support on 2026-05-20 (already past as of this writing)
systems.best_for: Historical reference only — do not build new integrations on this; it was the only fully-managed speaker-verification layer built directly into a hyperscaler's contact-center product
systems.watch: Fully ended: AWS's own documentation carries an end-of-support notice for 2026-05-20. Third-party coverage (ValidSoft) attributes the exit partly to real-world usability problems — the 30-second uninterrupted enrollment requirement struggled with noise, pauses, and interruptions in live call conditions.
systems.standout: Its exit, alongside Azure AI Speaker Recognition's retirement (Sept 30, 2025), completes a retreat of both AWS and Microsoft from native cloud speaker-verification products — it was the only fully-managed speaker-verification layer built directly into a hyperscaler's contact-center product.
systems.verification_note: End-of-support date and enrollment/verification mechanics confirmed directly on AWS's own Amazon Connect Voice ID admin documentation.

systems.name: Resemble Identity (Resemble AI)
systems.price_note: $0.0005 per identity search, pay-as-you-go; enterprise plans with custom SLA (99% uptime) also available
systems.method: Enrolls a speaker voiceprint from as little as 4 seconds of 16kHz audio (built on the vendor's open-source Resemblyzer d-vector encoder) and returns a match-distance score against enrolled profiles rather than a binary yes/no, so callers set their own accept threshold
systems.availability: Commercial REST API + web dashboard (cloud), with a containerized on-premises / air-gapped deployment option for enterprise plans
systems.best_for: Fraud/identity teams that want cloud speaker verification pairable with the same vendor's deepfake/voice-clone detector (Resemble Detect) in one pipeline
systems.watch: No published EER or accuracy figure for Identity itself — its output is a raw distance score you threshold yourself, so validate false-accept/false-reject rates on your own data before relying on it for high-stakes decisions
systems.standout: Pairs natively with Resemble Detect (the same vendor's synthetic-speech detector), so one vendor covers both 'is this the claimed speaker' and 'is this speech synthetic'
systems.verification_note: Pricing, enrollment mechanics, and deployment options are from Resemble AI's own product page; the 256-dimension embedding used by the underlying open-source Resemblyzer encoder is independently documented on its GitHub repo, but no independent accuracy benchmark for the commercial Identity product was located.

systems.name: pyannoteAI Voiceprints / Precision-2
systems.licence: Proprietary commercial API (built by the pyannote research team; the underlying pyannote-audio library remains separately MIT-licensed open source)
systems.price_note: Speaker Identification (matching a segment against a stored voiceprint) is billed at a flat €0.015 per match, same on both self-serve plans. Diarization on Precision-2 itself (a separate line item from identification) is €0.112/hour on the Developer plan and €0.096/hour on the Starter plan; Enterprise is volume-based. Voiceprint creation/enrollment is billed 'per voiceprint created, not per hour' per pyannoteAI's own pricing-calculator copy, but no public per-voiceprint rate is disclosed anywhere on the docs or pricing pages. Plans: Developer €19/mo, Starter €99/mo, Enterprise custom. Free trial includes 150 hours of identification + 10 voiceprints for one month.
systems.method: Enrolls a speaker voiceprint (embedding) from a reference clip via the Precision-2 model, then matches new audio against stored voiceprints for identification/verification; the free Community-1 model does not include this feature
systems.availability: Commercial hosted API only (pyannoteAI, the commercial successor built by the pyannote-audio research team)
systems.best_for: Developers already using pyannote's open-source diarization who want the same team's hosted, production-grade voiceprint/identification layer without operating their own GPU infrastructure
systems.watch: No public EER or accuracy benchmark for Precision-2's voiceprint/verification feature specifically — pyannoteAI publishes only a relative claim ('28% more accurate, on average, than Community-1') without naming a test set, and Community-1 (the free tier) explicitly lacks identification/voiceprints entirely
systems.standout: Built and maintained by the same research group behind the widely-used open-source pyannote-audio toolkit — unusual research pedigree for a commercial API in this category
systems.released: Precision-2 announced via pyannoteAI blog post "Setting a new standard with Precision-2" on Sep 1, 2025; changelog lists it as API-available Sep 2, 2025.
systems.verification_note: Pricing and the relative accuracy claim are pyannoteAI's own (pricing page, models page, Precision-2 launch blog); no absolute EER figure for voiceprint verification was found anywhere in the docs.

systems.name: IDVoice (ID R&D, now Mitek)
systems.price_note: Not publicly published — enterprise/custom licensing via sales contact
systems.method: Text-independent (and text-dependent) neural speaker-verification engine; enrolls a voiceprint from natural speech and matches new utterances against it, typically paired with ID R&D's own anti-spoofing/liveness layer
systems.availability: Commercial SDK that runs on customer premises (mobile, web, IVR/telephony, smart speakers, IoT/set-top boxes) as a standalone function, or as a cloud API; ID R&D was acquired by Mitek Systems in 2021
systems.best_for: Enterprises needing an embeddable, cross-channel (on-device SDK + server) speaker-verification engine with a track record on independently-run 'in the wild' benchmarks
systems.watch: Pricing and integration terms require a sales conversation — nothing is available for self-serve evaluation. Its VoxSRC wins are dated (2022, 2023); verify current standing yourself, since a challenge-year result does not guarantee the presently-shipping SDK version performs identically
systems.standout: Ranked #1 by both EER and detection-cost-function on the VoxCeleb Speaker Recognition Challenge (VoxSRC) 2023 public leaderboard (Track 2) — one of the few vendors here with a result judged in a third-party competition rather than self-reported alone
systems.benchmark_note: EER 1.30%, minDCF(0.05) 0.0762 — VoxCeleb Speaker Recognition Challenge (VoxSRC) 2023, Track 2, per the company's own system-description paper (arXiv:2308.08294); ranked #1 in both EER and DCF on the public leaderboard
systems.verification_note: The VoxSRC top ranking is independently corroborated by Biometric Update's reporting (Oct 2022 and Aug 2023) in addition to the vendor's own announcements, but the specific EER/minDCF figures trace to the company's own arXiv system-description paper rather than an official VoxSRC organizer scoreboard page.

systems.name: Phonexia Voice Verify
systems.licence: Proprietary commercial software (cloud or on-premises licensing)
systems.price_note: Not publicly published — custom quote via a Proof-of-Concept engagement through Phonexia's partner program
systems.method: Text-independent neural speaker-verification engine; enrolls a voiceprint from as little as ~3 seconds of free speech and scores subsequent audio against it
systems.availability: Commercial API/SDK deployable on-premises (documented multi-server topology requiring at least 10 VMs/physical servers) or via Phonexia's cloud
systems.best_for: Regulated or data-sovereignty-sensitive deployments (banks, government, telecom) that need speaker verification running entirely inside their own infrastructure rather than calling a public cloud API
systems.watch: No independent EER figure was located for the shipping Voice Verify product. The vendor's '96%+ accuracy out of the box after 3 seconds of speech' claim is measured on an undisclosed proprietary bank contact-center dataset (not a public/reproducible benchmark set) with no error-type (FAR/FRR) breakdown given, so treat it as marketing copy, not a benchmark result. Also note: Phonexia was acquired (full ownership) by Crescendo Equity Partners, a South Korea-based private equity firm, in December 2025, with the acquirer citing plans to expand the Europe-focused company into Asia amid rising deepfake/voice-fraud demand — a recent ownership change worth weighing for the data-sovereignty-sensitive buyers this row is pitched at.
systems.standout: One of the few vendors in this category built primarily around on-premises, multi-server deployment rather than a cloud-first API — relevant when customer voice data must never leave your own infrastructure
systems.benchmark_note: Phonexia's research team placed 2nd in the VoxCeleb Speaker Recognition Challenge (VoxSRC) 2021, Track 3, with EER 6.486% (arXiv:2109.02052) — a research-system result, not confirmed identical to the shipping Voice Verify product configuration
systems.verification_note: Deployment topology and pricing model are from Phonexia's own partner-portal documentation; the headline 96% accuracy figure is an unqualified vendor claim, while the VoxSRC 2021 EER is a genuine third-party-judged competition result but for a research system rather than the confirmed shipping product.

gaps: Resemblyzer and WeSpeaker were each independently discovered twice by the research pass, once under `metric` and once under `embedding-model` -- both are fundamentally embedding models you run yourself (not fixed-formula metrics), so each was merged into a single `embedding-model` row rather than publishing two disagreeing entries. A separate standalone `SECS` row already covers the metric/formula framing and credits Resemblyzer as its canonical encoder.

WeSpeaker's `released` year was disputed between the two audit passes (2022, from the repo's creation date/first tagged release, vs. 2023, from the ICASSP conference presentation date of its paper) -- resolved to 2022 for consistency with how this project dates other software toolkits by availability rather than paper-citation year.

SpeechBrain's ECAPA-TDNN checkpoint (speechbrain/spkrec-ecapa-voxceleb) was also independently discovered twice, once under `metric` (as 'SpeechBrain ECAPA-TDNN (spkrec-ecapa-voxceleb)') and once under `embedding-model` (as 'ECAPA-TDNN (SpeechBrain)') -- byte-identical source_url, same checkpoint, same reasoning as Resemblyzer/WeSpeaker above. Merged into a single `embedding-model` row, keeping the more complete method/benchmark_note detail from the `metric` instance (which more precisely attributes the 0.80%-with-normalization vs. 0.90%-without-normalization EER figures to two separate SpeechBrain documents) and the audit-corrected adoption figure (~1.7M HF downloads/month, not the ~3.4M an earlier draft of that row claimed) from the `embedding-model` instance.

`WavLM-TDNN speaker verification (Microsoft UniSpeech)` and `WavLM-Base-Plus-SV (Microsoft)` are the same Microsoft model family at two different checkpoint sizes -- the former's own `availability` text names the latter's exact checkpoint as its smaller variant. Deliberately kept as two rows rather than merged: they are genuinely different, independently downloadable checkpoints with different embedding dimensions and resource footprints (the size difference is the reason a reader would pick one over the other), unlike the artifact-of-research-pass duplicates merged above.
